title: For more parents, ‘vaccine refusal’ is becoming vaccine delay, but it’s no less dangerous
content: Vaccine refusal doesn’t always sound like vaccine refusal in my pediatric office anymore. More and more parents are delaying vaccines and citing logistics, outsourcing the decision to the parent who isn’t in the room or simply wanting more time. I hear countless variations, but the result is often the same: Children leave my office unvaccinated. “Oh, we’re definitely not anti-vaccine. We’re just waiting for Dad.” Dad comes to the next visit. “I think Mom should be here when we do them.” “We are definitely going to vaccinate but we have a birthday party coming up, doctor; wouldn’t want her to be under the weather!” Another parent agrees to the vaccines, then slips out of the office before the nurse returns with them because the child is “beside himself.” Minutes earlier the kid was happily playing in the exam room. Vaccination has become so socially and politically loaded that some parents don’t want to identify with either camp. Rather than explicitly refusing, they postpone. This is a worrisome trend. During the 2025–2026 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners in the United States had completed the recommended measles, mumps and rubella series, down from 95.2% in 2019–2020. A few percentage points may not sound like much, but it meant 280,000 kindergartners attended school without documentation that they had completed the series. As of early October, the US had recorded 4,080 confirmed cases of measles in 2026 and two deaths, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . Compare that with 2,289 cases and three deaths in all of 2025, and only 285 cases and no deaths in 2024. For me, and many of my pediatric colleagues I speak to regularly, it has led to a realization: If the problem is no longer always explicit refusal, then our interventions can’t be solely designed around convincing self-declared vaccine skeptics. We have to get better at responding to “not today,” and many of us, understanding what is at stake, are working hard to do so. When a parent tells me they’ll vaccinate next time, I respect that choice, but I’m also clear with them about what waiting means: Their child is leaving my office without protection against a disease we can prevent. I also believe when a parent says, “Maybe next time,” their doctor’s office should offer a date and time. “We’ll do it later” is an intention, while “we’ll be back on Tuesday at 3:30 p.m.” is a plan. It’s a way to make it as easy as possible to return to get the child protected without calling the parent out. Lately, I also talk to parents a lot more about the diseases we are aiming to prevent than I had in the past. Vaccines have been so successful that many of today’s parents and many young pediatricians have never seen what these diseases can do. Most parents have never watched a baby struggle through pertussis or rotavirus or seen a child hospitalized with complications of measles. When the disease feels theoretical and every alleged vaccine side effect is just one social media search away, how parents calculate risk can become distorted. Recent measles outbreaks are a painful reminder that these diseases did not disappear; we stopped seeing many of them because vaccines worked. I am also discussing vaccines as a normal part of preventive care, which they are. Instead of asking what parents want to do about vaccines during their child’s visit, I have shifted to the same assumption we bring to the rest of preventive care: “Your child is due for these vaccines today.” We discuss the risks and benefits that are part of any recommendation we make, and parents can, and should, still ask questions. They still make the ultimate decision. But in a world filled with falsehoods and other noise, clear communication goes a long way. In nuanced conversations that are far from black and white, I have also found myself tailoring my approach and getting creative. If one parent tells me she needs the other before deciding, we call the other parent together. If both parents truly need more time, then I make sure they leave with reliable information and are part of the next conversation. I have also included grandparents and have even sat through social media videos and group chat posts to answer everyone’s questions. We need our health systems to make saying “yes” to vaccines as easy as possible. That means improving access, streamlining workflows, and allowing more time for counseling parents with questions and concerns. What I see in my exam room makes me wonder whether there may be an emerging group of parents who genuinely support vaccines while actively choosing to delay them. To better understand how to support these parents, researchers need to study that gap, and research requires funding. For pediatricians like me to do our jobs, we need to understand how people actually make decisions about vaccines and how those decisions are changing. At the end of the day, however, I don’t particularly care whether a parent calls themselves pro- or anti-vaccine. Viruses and bacteria don’t care either. What matters is the protection against measles, mumps, rubella, influenza, chicken pox and more — not the label. For every child to be protected, they need to get their shots, today.
